claim.why_it_matters: The heading levels invert the clause hierarchy. 16.2.1.2 is a fourth-level clause but is emitted at h2 - shallower than its own parent 16.2.1 (h3) and shallower than its sibling 16.2.1.1 (h4). Likewise 16.2.2 (third level) is at h2 while its peer 16.2.1 is at h3, and 16.2.2.1 / 16.2.2.2 sit at h3 while their peer 16.2.1.1 sits at h4. Any tool that builds an outline, a TOC, or a section-anchored citation index from the headings places 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2 as top-level peers of the '## Page NNN' furniture rather than inside clause 16.2, so heading-tree citation lookup can fail to resolve 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2.x.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on four independent grounds. (Note: a prior verdict file existed at this path reaching the same real=false conclusion but citing heading statistics of '492 / 473 / 96%' that I could not reproduce. I recomputed them myself and replaced them with the verified figures below.) (1) NOTHING IS MISSING - the kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer. I rendered spec_p972.png at 300 dpi and read the printed page directly. It carries exactly four headings - '16.2.1.2 General rules', '16.2.2 FactoryObject method', '16.2.2.1 General', '16.2.2.2 General rule' - and all four are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md at lines 38833, 38840, 38843, 38848 with clause number and title verbatim, including the plural/singular distinction the PDF actually prints ('General rules' for 16.2.1.2, which carries two rules; 'General rule' for 16.2.2.2, which carries one). The claim quotes both sources accurately; it simply identifies no absent or altered content. Body text also matches word-for-word: both rules of 16.2.1.2 (including the '14.6.2.4, Initial state of object data' cross-reference and 'EC-OO-RESOURCE'), the 16.2.2.1 paragraph, rule 1) of 16.2.2.2, the NOTE, and all three Invoke example lines. (2) THE PDF ENCODES NO HEADING LEVEL TO LOSE. Looking at the printed glyphs myself: all four headings on this page are set in the SAME bold serif at the SAME point size, at the same left margin, with the same tab gap between number and title. '16.2.2 FactoryObject method' (third-level) is typographically indistinguishable from '16.2.2.1 General' (fourth-level). ISO conveys clause depth here through the dotted NUMBER alone - and the markdown preserves that number exactly in every heading. A markdown '#' count therefore transcribes nothing that exists in the source, so a 'wrong' count cannot be a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Per the standing rejection criteria this is formatting, and it changes no meaning. (3) THE PATTERN IS A DOCUMENT-WIDE CONVERSION ARTIFACT, NOT A PAGE-972 DEFECT. The transcription is page-sliced and the converter restarts heading depth at each slice, having no cross-page context. Verified over the whole file: 594 numbered headings are the first numbered heading following a '## Page NNN' marker; 521 of them (88%) are emitted at h2, and 420 (71%) are shallower than their clause depth implies. 16.2.1.2 at line 38833 is precisely such a heading - the first one after the page-972 marker at line 38828. Aggregate tallies confirm heading depth is not a function of clause depth anywhere in the file: 4-component clauses split 162/620/24 across h2/h3/h4, 3-component clauses split 276/508/17, 5-component clauses split 118/128/41, and 1345 numbered headings file-wide sit shallower than their component count. Page 972 is one unremarkable instance of a global artifact; ledgering it as a page-972 structural discrepancy would misattribute a whole-document formatting convention to this page. (4) THE CLAIM'S OWN BASELINE IS SELF-DEFEATING, AND THE ASSERTED HARM DOES NOT OCCUR. The claim treats lines 38819/38822 as the correct hierarchy, but that baseline is broken by the same convention it appeals to: '## 16 Standard classes' (line 38782, one component) sits at h2 while '### 16.2 BASE class' (line 38790, two components) and '### 16.2.1 New method' (three components) both sit at h3 - parent and child at equal depth. There is no consistent local convention to violate. And the stated failure mode - 'heading-tree citation lookup can fail to resolve 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2.x' - is not reachable: every heading on the page is immediately preceded by an explicit anchor encoding the full clause path (line 38832 '', 38839 'section-16-2-2', 38842 'section-16-2-2-1', 38847 'section-16-2-2-2'). Those anchors, plus the dotted number inside the heading text, make the hierarchy fully machine-recoverable independent of '#' depth. The only textual difference found anywhere on the page is that the PDF NOTE sets a double space in 'the methods of a factory object' where the markdown has one - pure whitespace, explicitly out of scope. No content discrepancy exists on page 972.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy; no heading is missing. All four headings (16.2.1.2, 16.2.2, 16.2.2.1, 16.2.2.2) are present with correct numbers and titles, and the page body matches the PDF word-for-word. The PDF sets every heading on this page in identical bold type at identical size and conveys hierarchy solely through the dotted clause number, which the markdown preserves - so there is no source-side heading level that transcription could have lost or inverted. The uneven '#' depths are a document-wide side effect of page-sliced conversion resetting heading depth at each page boundary: 521 of the 594 numbered headings that follow a '## Page NNN' marker (88%) are emitted at h2, and heading depth does not track clause depth anywhere in the file (4-component clauses alone split 162/620/24 across h2/h3/h4). The claim's own reference points show the same effect ('## 16' at h2 above '### 16.2' and '### 16.2.1' both at h3), so it has no valid baseline. The asserted citation-lookup failure does not occur, because explicit '<a id="section-16-2-1-2">', 'section-16-2-2', 'section-16-2-2-1' and 'section-16-2-2-2' anchors precede the headings and encode the full clause path. If uniform heading depth is wanted, it is a single global normalization pass over the transcription pipeline (derive level from the dotted clause number), tracked as transcription quality - not a page-972 reconciliation finding.
